hero.headline: St. Lucie County sends 30-day removal notices to 50-55 license plate camera permit holders
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County has notified all automated license plate reader permit holders that they have 30 days to remove cameras from county rights-of-way. The county will remove non-compliant units itself if permit holders fail to act.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sent letters earlier this week to all automated license plate reader permit holders, giving them 30 days to remove the cameras from county-maintained roads. Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County, said the county issued about 50 to 55 permits for the cameras, including Flock cameras.

 The letters went to permit holders that submitted permits on behalf of law enforcement agencies and directly to camera manufacturers. County rights-of-way include the shoulders of highways and roads maintained by the county. If permit holders fail to remove the cameras within the 30-day period, county staff will step in to remove them. Gill said permit owners will likely want to handle the removal themselves because the cameras have value and could be damaged, and the permit holders originally did the installations.

 County staff provided the updates to commissioners during a meeting following a vote earlier this month. St. Lucie County residents expressed opposition to the surveillance cameras. Toria Hoke said she thinks the cameras are too intrusive and might impede freedom.

 Herman Felton said the cameras are spying on people, though he acknowledged they could be useful in certain situations. Felton raised concerns about privacy, saying people have a right to privacy and whatever they are doing at their house is their business.

 County leaders clarified that the removal of the cameras from public roads does not mean they are banned entirely. Cameras can still be installed on private property or non-maintained rights-of-way.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies use helicopter to capture Lake Worth man after high-speed liquor theft chase
cards.teaser: A Lake Worth man was arrested after he allegedly stole liquor from a Martin County Publix and fled from deputies at speeds exceeding 80 mph before being tracked by helicopter into
cards.body:
A Lake Worth man was arrested after he allegedly stole liquor from a Martin County Publix and fled from deputies at speeds exceeding 80 mph before being tracked by helicopter into Palm Beach County. Derwyn Don Edwards, 24, was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol and faces charges of reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft.

 According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. and stole multiple bottles of liquor. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving.

 A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but authorities said Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly. Because the incident did not meet the agency's pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged.

 Deputies said Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95. MCSO Air 1 then located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody.

 Edwards is being held at the Martin County Jail.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County sends 30-day removal notices to 50-55 license plate camera permit holders
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County has notified all automated license plate reader permit holders that they have 30 days to remove cameras from county rights-of-way. The county will remove non-compliant units itself if permit holders fail to act.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sent letters earlier this week to all automated license plate reader permit holders, giving them 30 days to remove the cameras from county-maintained roads. Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County, said the county issued about 50 to 55 permits for the cameras, including Flock cameras.

 The letters went to permit holders that submitted permits on behalf of law enforcement agencies and directly to camera manufacturers. County rights-of-way include the shoulders of highways and roads maintained by the county. If permit holders fail to remove the cameras within the 30-day period, county staff will step in to remove them. Gill said permit owners will likely want to handle the removal themselves because the cameras have value and could be damaged, and the permit holders originally did the installations.

 County staff provided the updates to commissioners during a meeting following a vote earlier this month. St. Lucie County residents expressed opposition to the surveillance cameras. Toria Hoke said she thinks the cameras are too intrusive and might impede freedom.

 Herman Felton said the cameras are spying on people, though he acknowledged they could be useful in certain situations. Felton raised concerns about privacy, saying people have a right to privacy and whatever they are doing at their house is their business.

 County leaders clarified that the removal of the cameras from public roads does not mean they are banned entirely. Cameras can still be installed on private property or non-maintained rights-of-way.
